prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform the large-volume lumbar tap before brain MRI has excluded a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus

Do not diagnose iNPH from ventriculomegaly alone: the diagnosis needs the clinical syndrome (gait disturbance with cognitive or urinary symptoms) and supportive imaging, with no other cause explaining them [Relkin_2005]
Do not attribute the urge incontinence to benign prostatic hyperplasia alone and leave it out of the gait and cognitive syndrome
Do not attribute the syndrome to normal ageing or deconditioning once the ventriculomegaly and the tap response are documented
required_recommendations: Refer to neurosurgery for CSF shunting with a programmable valve, on the basis of the tap-test improvement of 32% in TUG at 24 hours, the DESH MRI (Evans index 0.38, callosal angle 74 degrees) and normal-pressure CSF [Nakajima_2021]
Counsel that gait is the symptom most likely to improve after shunting, and that the urge incontinence may be mixed with benign prostatic hyperplasia, so its response is less predictable
Falls-prevention measures (physiotherapy, home assessment, walking aid) while awaiting surgery, given two falls in 6 months

avoided_actions.rationale: He has no episodes suggesting seizures, so an EEG cannot help separate iNPH from its mimics.
His two falls were trips without syncope or palpitations, so an ECG does not inform the gait work-up.
There is no syncope, murmur or embolic event, so echocardiography has no role in this work-up.
He already had a CT; MRI measures the callosal angle, temporal horns and aqueduct better and is available.
The falls are not syncopal, so rhythm monitoring has no diagnostic role here.
Molecular or advanced imaging does not change the iNPH decision, which rests on MRI and the tap test
A full neuropsychological battery is not needed for the iNPH decision; the bedside screen and timed gait measures are
Normal-pressure CSF with a normal cell count in a two-year afebrile gait syndrome gives no indication for prion, inflammatory or infectious assays.

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / subcortical ischaemic vascular disease
differential.key_features: White matter change is only Fazekas 1, far less than the ventriculomegaly, and the gait improves after the tap.
Shuffling and freezing overlap, but there is no rest tremor, rigidity or asymmetry, and the gait responds to CSF removal.
Getting lost and a family history raise it, but recall improves with cues within a dysexecutive profile, the hippocampi are MTA 1 and gait led the syndrome.

differential.diagnosis: Cerebral atrophy with secondary ex-vacuo ventriculomegaly
differential.key_features: Ventricles are enlarged out of proportion to the sulci, with DESH and a callosal angle of 74 degrees, and the gait improves after the tap.

differential.diagnosis: Secondary communicating hydrocephalus (post-traumatic, post-haemorrhagic or post-meningitic)
differential.key_features: No head injury, subarachnoid haemorrhage or meningitis in the history.

key_clinical_evidence: Probable iNPH needs an insidious gait disturbance after age 40 lasting at least 3 to 6 months with cognitive or urinary symptoms, no antecedent cause, ventriculomegaly (Evans index greater than 0.3) not explained by atrophy, and a CSF opening pressure of 5 to 18 mmHg (7 to 24.5 cmH2O) [Relkin_2005].
DESH and an acute callosal angle support the diagnosis; here Evans 0.38, DESH and a callosal angle of 74 degrees [Nakajima_2021].

The tap test removes 30 to 50 mL and repeats the timed gait measures at 2 to 4 and 24 hours [Nakajima_2021]; a 10% or greater TUG improvement is a commonly used positive threshold, though no guideline sets a single cut-off. Its sensitivity is 26% to 61% and its PPV 73% to 100%, so a single negative tap does not exclude shunt-responsive iNPH [Marmarou_2005].
Urge incontinence in an older man with BPH can be mixed; failure of a higher tamsulosin dose and onset with the gait decline point to the iNPH syndrome.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: BPH may contribute, but urge incontinence that did not respond to a higher tamsulosin dose and arose with the gait and cognitive decline fits iNPH; the urinary symptoms are probably mixed.
red_herrings.data_point: Benign prostatic hyperplasia on tamsulosin, with the urinary urgency first attributed to it and no benefit from a dose increase
red_herrings.intended_effect: The urinary urgency is attributed to BPH, so the urinary component of the syndrome is discounted

sequence_constraints.reason: Brain imaging must exclude a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus before CSF is removed [Relkin_2005]
The baseline gait must be measured before the tap, or the post-tap change cannot be interpreted [Nakajima_2021]
The timed gait is repeated after the tap, at 2 to 24 hours, so that its change from the baseline measures the response to CSF removal [Nakajima_2021]

patient.history_present_illness: A 76-year-old right-handed retired postal worker with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and BPH was admitted for evaluation of progressive gait and cognitive decline. His wife first noticed a change in his walking approximately two years ago, describing it as a 'slow shuffle' with short steps and occasional freezing near doorways. He has had two falls in the past six months, once in the bathroom and once stepping off a curb. He now uses a cane for outdoor ambulation and requires physical assistance on stairs. Over the same two-year period, he has become increasingly forgetful: he misplaces items, loses track of conversations, and recently became lost while driving to a grocery store he had visited for twenty years. His wife notes that he is slower to respond in conversation and that his personality has become slightly flat. He has experienced escalating urinary urgency over the past eighteen months, with near-daily episodes of urge incontinence. He initially attributed this to his known BPH and his tamsulosin dose was increased without benefit. There is no headache, vomiting, diplopia, limb weakness, or sensory loss. He denies tremor at rest. A head CT obtained three months ago by his primary care physician was reported as showing enlarged ventricles; the images are not available. He was referred by his primary care physician for progressive gait difficulty with memory decline and urinary urgency.

neurological_exam.additional: No nuchal rigidity. Frontal release signs: grasp reflex present bilaterally, snout reflex present.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Normal. No papilledema. Extraocular movements intact.
neurological_exam.gait: Wide-based, magnetic, shuffling gait with short steps and reduced step height. En-bloc turning. Unable to tandem walk. Pull test: two steps back.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented to person, place and date. Slowed responses, reduced spontaneous speech. No aphasia. Formal cognitive screening reported separately.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal tone and bulk. Full strength bilaterally. No tremor at rest. No rigidity.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch, pinprick, and proprioception intact throughout.
